sections.heading: Why chores matter at age 6
sections.body:
Around their sixth birthday, most children have the motor skills and attention span to complete simple household tasks from start to finish — without a grown-up finishing it for them. Research on child development consistently shows that children who do regular chores develop stronger executive function, a greater sense of belonging in the family, and better self-regulation skills later in life.

The key is to match the chore to what the child can actually do today, then step back and let them own it — even if the bed isn't perfectly straight. Mastery and pride in a job done matter far more than perfection.

sections.heading: What these chores teach
sections.body: Making the bed and tidying the bedroom teach ownership of personal space — two minutes each morning that build a life-long habit. Setting the table and feeding a pet give children a meaningful role in caring for others, which research links to greater empathy. Watering the plants and sorting laundry by colour develop patience and an eye for pattern — cognitive skills that transfer well into schoolwork.

sections.heading: Tips for making chores stick
sections.body:
- Do it together the first few times — demonstration beats instruction every time at this age.
- Put the chart where it's visible — print it and stick it on the fridge or bedroom door, not a buried bookmark.
- Tick the boxes together each evening; the ritual of checking off tasks is motivating in itself.
- Adjust the list as skills grow — by age 7 or 8, most children are ready to load the dishwasher or take out the bins.

faq.a: A typical 6-year-old can make their bed, set the table, feed a pet, tidy their room, water plants, and sort laundry by colour — tasks they can finish independently with a little initial guidance.

faq.q: Should a 6-year-old be paid for chores?
faq.a: In our house, everyday family chores aren't paid — they're simply part of belonging to the family. We do pay a small weekly allowance from about age five or six, but it's tied to doing the work well and with a good attitude, not to any single task. That way kids learn responsibility first and earning second.
